candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest labels this binary MALWARE with probability 0.67, which is only moderately above the decision boundary. All 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, but the contributions are small and nearly flat (+0.0051 to +0.0089), so no single feature dominates. Most of the n-grams are also very rare, with relative frequencies from 0.000045 to 0.002247. The evidence has three themes. (1) Bit-manipulation and integer patterns (ROR MOV at +0.008916, AND ROR at +0.005395, AND SUB at +0.007097, AND SAR at +0.005730, MOV XCHG at +0.005161) could resemble hash or cipher mixing, but they are low-frequency and common in general compiled code. (2) SSE byte-scan patterns (PCMPEQB PMOVMSKB, XORPS PCMPEQB, BSF MOV, BSF SUB, PSRLDQ XORPS) look like vectorized string or memory scanning, and this is not specific to mining. (3) Scalar double-precision and FMA patterns (VSUBSD VSUBSD, VMOVSD VFMADD213SD, VMULSD VFMADD213SD, MOVAPD DIVSD, MULSD MOVAPD) suggest floating-point math, which is typical of compiler runtime or math library code and not a proof of mining. The evidence lists no function names or call context, so none of these patterns can be tied to a mining loop, a stratum-style workload, or a sustained compute kernel. The patterns are consistent with cryptojacking code but equally consistent with benign code, so the case is inconclusive. The confidence_score is my estimated likelihood of cryptojacking, not certainty in the tier.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Rotate followed by move is a building block of hash and cipher rounds, so it is the strongest single hint toward mining-style mixing. At a frequency of only 0.000854 it is not a sustained hashing kernel, and rotates also occur in ordinary runtime code.
An SSE byte shift followed by an XOR is used in vectorized data mixing and register clearing. It is weakly consistent with crypto-style vector work but generic, and its frequency is low.

Consecutive AVX scalar double subtractions indicate floating-point numeric code. Integer-heavy miners do not typically rely on this, so it is likely incidental math or library code. The frequency is extremely low (0.000045).
Bit-scan-forward is commonly used to find the first matching byte after a vector compare, as in optimized string or memory routines. It is not specific to mining.
This is a classic SSE2 idiom for byte comparison and mask extraction, used in strlen, memchr and similar routines. It is characteristic of generic library code and weak evidence for cryptojacking.
A common integer masking and arithmetic pair at a relatively high frequency (0.001393). It points to ordinary alignment or index arithmetic and has little discriminative value for mining.
Register zeroing followed by a byte compare is part of the vectorized scan idiom seen with PCMPEQB PMOVMSKB and BSF. It most likely belongs to the same string or memory routine and not to a miner.
This is another bit-scan idiom that computes an offset or length after a vector match. It is likely tied to the same scanning routines and is not indicative of mining.
XOR followed by NOP is likely register zeroing before padding or alignment. It carries no meaningful cryptojacking signal despite the SHAP weight.
A counter decrement with a conditional exit is a generic loop-control pattern. It could belong to a hashing loop but is equally common everywhere.
An integer add followed by a transfer between general-purpose and XMM registers is a generic data movement pattern. It is not specific to mining.
An address computation followed by a stack pop is typical of function epilogues. This is a compiler artifact with no cryptojacking significance.

An AVX scalar load followed by a fused multiply-add indicates floating-point polynomial or math-library evaluation. Floating-point FMA is not typical of integer hashing miners, so this is weak or incidental evidence.
A mask-and-shift pair at a relatively high frequency (0.002247). It reflects common bit-field or arithmetic handling and is not discriminative for mining.
A scalar multiply followed by an FMA is a floating-point math pattern, consistent with numeric library routines. It does not indicate a mining kernel.
A packed-double move followed by a scalar double division is generic floating-point computation at a very low frequency. It has no clear link to cryptojacking.

A mask followed by a rotate is mildly suggestive of hash-style bit mixing and appears alongside ROR MOV. At a frequency of 0.001259 it is still not conclusive and also appears in benign hashing or checksum code.
An exchange after a move is typical of swap or synchronization-style operations. It is ambiguous and not indicative of mining by itself.
A scalar double multiply followed by a register move is ordinary floating-point code. It adds little cryptojacking signal.

SSE byte unpacking and shuffling are used in vectorized data reformatting. They can occur in crypto or hash implementations but are also common in memory and string routines. The frequency is very low.
